subject: Biology
title: Flowers and Their Pollinators
description: A 60-second lesson on Flowers and Their Pollinators.

hook.text: Darwin saw an orchid with a 30 cm nectar tube and predicted a moth with a 30 cm tongue must exist. It did.

buildup.text: Co-evolution occurs when two species reciprocally drive each other's adaptation over time.

discovery.text: Flowers evolved colors, shapes, and scents matched to specific pollinators—bees, birds, bats, or moths.

twist.text: Red flowers attract hummingbirds but are invisible to bees. Night-blooming white flowers attract moths.

climax.text: This tight mutual dependence means losing one partner can drive the other to extinction.

punchline.text: Darwin predicted a moth from a flower. Co-evolution is that precise.

quiz.question: What did Darwin predict from seeing a 30 cm orchid nectar tube?
options: A moth with a 30 cm tongue must exist
The orchid was a different species

details.summary: Flowers and pollinators have coevolved over 130 million years, producing remarkable mutual adaptations. Flowers evolved colors, scents, shapes, and nectar rewards to attract specific pollinators, while pollinators evolved specialized bodies and behaviors to access these rewards.
details.whyItMatters: Pollinator coevolution shaped the diversity of flowering plants that dominate terrestrial ecosystems. Disrupting these partnerships through habitat loss or pollinator decline threatens both plant reproduction and associated ecosystem services.
takeaways: Red tubular flowers evolved to attract hummingbirds with no landing platform
Night-blooming flowers use strong scent to attract moth and bat pollinators
Orchids sometimes deceive pollinators with fake rewards or pheromone mimicry

faq.question: How do flowers attract specific pollinators?
faq.answer: Pollination syndromes match flower traits to pollinator preferences. Bee flowers are blue or yellow with nectar guides. Bird flowers are red and tubular. Bat flowers open at night with strong musky scents. These trait combinations direct the right pollinator to each flower.

faq.question: Why do some orchids trick their pollinators?
faq.answer: Deceptive pollination avoids the energy cost of producing nectar. Some orchids mimic female insect pheromones or appearances, luring males to attempt mating and inadvertently transfer pollen. Others resemble rewarding flowers without actually offering any food.
